problem.title: Frog Jump (Min Energy 1D DP)

fields.name: heights
fields.label: Stair heights
fields.help: Energy for a jump is the height difference, so a tall stair next door can cost more than a short one two away.

problem.description: Find min energy for frog to reach stair N-1 jumping 1 or 2 stairs.
statement: A frog stands on stair 0 of a staircase with n stairs, numbered 0 to n − 1. The array heights gives the height of each stair.
From stair i the frog may jump to stair i + 1 or stair i + 2, as long as that stair exists. A jump from stair i to stair j costs |heights[i] − heights[j]| energy.
Return the minimum total energy the frog needs to reach stair n − 1.

examples.explanation: Jump 0 → 2 for |40 − 10| = 30, then 2 → 3 for |30 − 40| = 10, a total of 40. Any route through stair 1 already costs 40 on its first jump and more after it.
Jump 0 → 1 for 20, 1 → 3 for 0 (both stairs have height 10), and 3 → 4 for 10, a total of 30.

steps.description: The frog starts on stair 0 and must reach stair 3. energy[i] will hold the cheapest total cost of standing on stair i.
Stair 0 costs nothing — the frog is already there, having jumped nowhere.
Stair 1 has only one predecessor, so there is nothing to compare against: energy[0] + |50 - 10| = 40.

Stair 2: a 1-step from 1 costs 40 + |40 - 50| = 50; a 2-step from 0 costs 0 + |40 - 10| = 30. energy[2] = 30 — the 2-step wins. What decides it is the running total, not the height gap, so skipping a stair can beat hopping to the nearest.
Stair 3: a 1-step from 2 costs 30 + |30 - 40| = 40; a 2-step from 1 costs 40 + |30 - 50| = 60. energy[3] = 40 — the 1-step wins.
Cheapest way onto stair 3 is 40 energy. Note the frog never needed to know which route it took — only the cost of the best one.
